questions.prompt: Complaints may come face to face, by phone or by ______

questions.explanation: Paragraph D says anything beyond refunds and replacements, such as travel costs or goodwill vouchers, needs a supervisor's approval.

questions.prompt: Complaints log: record the customer's own ______ of the issue
questions.evidence: using the customer's own description of the problem
questions.explanation: Paragraph E says staff should use the customer's own description of the problem, not their own summary.

questions.prompt: According to the booklet, customers who complain usually

have already decided to leave the company.
would rather write an email than phone.

questions.evidence: Customers who bother to complain are usually telling us that they want to keep doing business with us
questions.explanation: Paragraph A says complaining customers want to keep doing business with the company. It is customers who are finished with a company who leave without saying anything.

questions.prompt: Why should staff repeat the customer's main points back to them?

options.text: to gain time to think of a solution
to let the customer put right any error
to create a record for the complaints log
to defend the company against the complaint

questions.evidence: it gives the customer a chance to correct any misunderstanding before you act on it
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says repeating the points gives the customer a chance to correct any misunderstanding. The booklet actually tells staff not to defend the company at this stage.

questions.prompt: What does the writer say about acknowledging a customer's feelings?

options.text: It should come only after an investigation.
It must always include a formal apology.
It does not mean admitting the company was wrong.
It matters less than offering a quick solution.

questions.evidence: This is not the same as admitting that the company is at fault.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says acknowledging feelings is different from admitting fault. An apology is only needed if a mistake is actually found.

questions.prompt: Which of the following may any member of staff do without a supervisor's approval?

options.text: pay back the cost of a customer's journey
give the customer a goodwill voucher
agree compensation for the customer's lost time
refund a recent purchase with proof of payment

questions.evidence: give a full refund on items bought within the last thirty days, provided the customer can show a receipt or a bank statement
questions.explanation: Paragraph D allows all staff to give a refund on items bought within thirty days if there is a receipt or bank statement. Travel costs, vouchers and any other compensation need a supervisor's approval.

questions.prompt: What did Ilse Mbatha's review of complaint records show?

options.text: Most complaints were settled within two working days.
Updates helped only when they contained new information.
Customers kept informed early were less likely to take things further.
The branches that replied fastest received the fewest complaints.

questions.evidence: customers who received an update before the deadline, even one saying only that the investigation was still going on, were much less likely to escalate their complaint
questions.explanation: Paragraph E reports that customers who got an update before the deadline were much less likely to escalate. This was true even when the update gave no news, so the option about updates needing new information is wrong.

questions.prompt: What does Callixte Duarte advise staff to do after a difficult conversation?

options.text: take a short break before the next customer
write down what happened straight away
ask a supervisor to take over the next call
give the customer one clear final warning

questions.evidence: recommends taking a few minutes away from your desk after any difficult exchange
questions.explanation: Paragraph F says Duarte recommends spending a few minutes away from the desk. Writing an account is general advice from the booklet, not his recommendation.

questions.prompt: Why should staff choose the category for a closed complaint carefully?

options.text: It decides how fast a complaint can be closed.
Customers can see it on their own records.
Supervisors use it to judge individual staff.
It helps managers notice problems that keep recurring.

questions.evidence: several of the improvements introduced over the past year, including clearer labels on our returns envelopes, began as patterns that front-line staff had noticed and recorded
questions.explanation: Paragraph G says team leaders read the categories every month, and that several improvements started as patterns staff had recorded. Nothing is said about judging staff or customers seeing the categories.

blocks.instruction: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

people.name: Ilse Mbatha
people.role: manager of the customer service team who reviewed six months of complaint records

people.name: Callixte Duarte
people.role: senior trainer who advises taking a break after difficult exchanges

paragraphs.text: Every complaint, however unpleasant it may feel at the time, is a chance to put something right. Customers who bother to complain are usually telling us that they want to keep doing business with us; those who are truly finished with a company tend to leave without a word. This section of the booklet explains what you need to know before a complaint reaches you and what you should do once it has. It applies whether the customer speaks to you face to face, phones the helpline or writes to us by email.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Your first task is simply to listen. Many staff feel pressure to offer a solution within seconds, but interrupting a customer who is still explaining the problem almost always makes matters worse. Let the person finish, even if you think you already know what they are going to say. Do not be tempted to defend the company at this stage. Take brief notes as they talk, and when they have finished, repeat the main points back to them in your own words. This shows that you have understood, and it gives the customer a chance to correct any misunderstanding before you act on it.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Next, acknowledge how the customer feels. This is not the same as admitting that the company is at fault. A sentence such as "I can see why that would be frustrating" recognises the customer's experience without accepting blame for something that has not yet been investigated. Avoid phrases like "calm down" or "that's our policy", which tend to sound dismissive even when they are not meant to. If you do discover that we have made a mistake, however, say so plainly and apologise; customers are far more forgiving of an honest error than of an excuse.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Before you promise anything, check what you are allowed to offer. All staff may replace faulty goods or give a full refund on items bought within the last thirty days, provided the customer can show a receipt or a bank statement. Anything beyond this, such as compensation for travel costs or a goodwill voucher, must be approved by a supervisor. Never promise an outcome you are not certain you can deliver: a broken promise turns one complaint into two. If you need to pass the matter on, tell the customer who will deal with it and when they can expect to hear back.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Some complaints cannot be settled during the first conversation. In these cases, record the details on the complaints log the same day, using the customer's own description of the problem rather than a summary of your own. Our policy is to send a written acknowledgement within two working days and a full response within ten. Ilse Mbatha, who manages our customer service team, reviewed six months of records last year and found that customers who received an update before the deadline, even one saying only that the investigation was still going on, were much less likely to escalate their complaint. Her review covered only our own branches, but its message is clear: silence is usually read as indifference.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Occasionally a customer becomes aggressive. You are not expected to put up with abuse. Stay calm, keep your voice low and steady, and explain politely that you want to help but cannot continue if the shouting goes on. If the behaviour continues, you may end a phone call after one clear warning, or ask a supervisor to take over a face-to-face conversation. Afterwards, write a short account of what happened while it is fresh in your mind. Callixte Duarte, our senior trainer, recommends taking a few minutes away from your desk after any difficult exchange, since carrying tension into the next conversation can affect how you treat a customer who has done nothing wrong.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: Finally, remember that each complaint contains information. A single complaint about a late delivery may be bad luck; ten in a week suggest a problem with a supplier or a route. When you close a complaint on the log, choose the category that best describes the cause, not merely the symptom. Team leaders read these categories every month, and several of the improvements introduced over the past year, including clearer labels on our returns envelopes, began as patterns that front-line staff had noticed and recorded. The few seconds it takes to choose carefully are well spent.
paragraphs.label: G

section.text:
Handling Complaints: A Guide for Front-Line Staff

A. Every complaint, however unpleasant it may feel at the time, is a chance to put something right. Customers who bother to complain are usually telling us that they want to keep doing business with us; those who are truly finished with a company tend to leave without a word. This section of the booklet explains what you need to know before a complaint reaches you and what you should do once it has. It applies whether the customer speaks to you face to face, phones the helpline or writes to us by email.

B. Your first task is simply to listen. Many staff feel pressure to offer a solution within seconds, but interrupting a customer who is still explaining the problem almost always makes matters worse. Let the person finish, even if you think you already know what they are going to say. Do not be tempted to defend the company at this stage. Take brief notes as they talk, and when they have finished, repeat the main points back to them in your own words. This shows that you have understood, and it gives the customer a chance to correct any misunderstanding before you act on it.

C. Next, acknowledge how the customer feels. This is not the same as admitting that the company is at fault. A sentence such as "I can see why that would be frustrating" recognises the customer's experience without accepting blame for something that has not yet been investigated. Avoid phrases like "calm down" or "that's our policy", which tend to sound dismissive even when they are not meant to. If you do discover that we have made a mistake, however, say so plainly and apologise; customers are far more forgiving of an honest error than of an excuse.

D. Before you promise anything, check what you are allowed to offer. All staff may replace faulty goods or give a full refund on items bought within the last thirty days, provided the customer can show a receipt or a bank statement. Anything beyond this, such as compensation for travel costs or a goodwill voucher, must be approved by a supervisor. Never promise an outcome you are not certain you can deliver: a broken promise turns one complaint into two. If you need to pass the matter on, tell the customer who will deal with it and when they can expect to hear back.

E. Some complaints cannot be settled during the first conversation. In these cases, record the details on the complaints log the same day, using the customer's own description of the problem rather than a summary of your own. Our policy is to send a written acknowledgement within two working days and a full response within ten. Ilse Mbatha, who manages our customer service team, reviewed six months of records last year and found that customers who received an update before the deadline, even one saying only that the investigation was still going on, were much less likely to escalate their complaint. Her review covered only our own branches, but its message is clear: silence is usually read as indifference.

F. Occasionally a customer becomes aggressive. You are not expected to put up with abuse. Stay calm, keep your voice low and steady, and explain politely that you want to help but cannot continue if the shouting goes on. If the behaviour continues, you may end a phone call after one clear warning, or ask a supervisor to take over a face-to-face conversation. Afterwards, write a short account of what happened while it is fresh in your mind. Callixte Duarte, our senior trainer, recommends taking a few minutes away from your desk after any difficult exchange, since carrying tension into the next conversation can affect how you treat a customer who has done nothing wrong.

G. Finally, remember that each complaint contains information. A single complaint about a late delivery may be bad luck; ten in a week suggest a problem with a supplier or a route. When you close a complaint on the log, choose the category that best describes the cause, not merely the symptom. Team leaders read these categories every month, and several of the improvements introduced over the past year, including clearer labels on our returns envelopes, began as patterns that front-line staff had noticed and recorded. The few seconds it takes to choose carefully are well spent.

explanation.uk: В абзаці B працівникам радять робити стислі нотатки, поки клієнт говорить; «short» передає зміст слова «brief».

explanation.uk: В абзаці C сказано, що, визнаючи почуття клієнта, працівник визнає його досвід, але не бере на себе провину.

explanation.uk: В абзаці D сказано, що повне повернення коштів протягом тридцяти днів дозволене, якщо клієнт може показати чек або банківську виписку.

explanation.uk: В абзаці D сказано, що все, окрім повернення коштів і заміни товару, наприклад витрати на дорогу чи ваучери як жест доброї волі, потребує схвалення керівника.
